title: Machines that learn to read
text: Machine translation has travelled from a joke to a {{1}} in under a decade. The older systems translated phrase by phrase, producing sentences that a native reader could {{2}} only with sympathy; the modern ones, trained on millions of translated documents, produce prose that is routinely fluent and frequently {{3}}. This leap did not come from better rules about language — it came from abandoning rules almost entirely. Given enough examples, a statistical model {{4}} the patterns of good translation for itself, which is why it excels at the {{5}} phrases that grammar books struggle to explain: 'out of the blue', 'by and large', 'set store by'. The limitations are equally instructive. The systems have no model of the world, so an ambiguous sentence comes out one way or another and a {{6}} editor must decide. Literary translation, dialect, humour and anything that {{7}} on what is left unsaid remain stubbornly human. Professional translators have not vanished; their work has moved up the value chain, {{8}} machine output rather than producing first drafts, and specialising in exactly the texts where the machines are weakest.

gaps.explanation: 'from a joke to a contender' — a genuine rival; conductor = an orchestra leader or a train official.
'could comprehend only with sympathy' — barely understand; compromise = settle or weaken.
'frequently accurate' — correct; abrupt = sudden, arid = dry.
'a model acquires the patterns for itself' — learns them from examples; adjudicate = judge a dispute.
'fixed phrases that grammar books struggle to explain' — the linguistic term for set expressions like 'out of the blue'.
'a human editor must decide' — a person; humane = compassionate, a different word entirely.
'anything that depends on what is left unsaid' — hinges on it; spend takes money or time as its object.
'polishing machine output rather than producing first drafts' — improving and refining it; perish = die.
